title: Life and dignity
hook: a psalm looks at the stars, then at people, and finds a crown

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catholic social teaching: a body of teaching, not one book. Your line was love, organized. Did one problem show you its root? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.

A psalm stands under the night sky, looks at the moon and the stars, and asks a question. In the Douay-Rheims: "What is man that thou art mindful of him?" Next to all that sky, a person looks small. Then the psalm answers its own question, and the answer goes the other way: "Thou hast made him a little less than the angels, thou hast crowned him with glory and honour." Not small after all. Crowned. Catholic social teaching sets that crown on every head before it says a word about wages or laws. Today, life and dignity.
screen: `THE MOON, THE STARS, AND A PERSON.` → `WHAT IS MAN?` → `CROWNED WITH GLORY.`

segments.voice: First, the root. Genesis says, in the Douay-Rheims: "God created man to his own image." Catholics read that line as the ground under this whole block. Dignity isn't a prize a society hands out. It comes with being human. Second, what follows: it isn't earned, and it can't be lost. Not by being unproductive, or sick, or old, or poor, or in prison, or not yet born. The Catechism, quoting the Second Vatican Council, says God willed each human being for their own sake, not as a tool for something else. Third, the span. The Church teaches that every human life is to be protected from conception to natural death. That's why Catholic teaching opposes abortion and euthanasia, and why the Catechism now calls the death penalty inadmissible. The same council also named slavery, the selling of women and children, and disgraceful working conditions as attacks on human dignity. Some Catholics give their energy to one end of that span and some to another; the teaching holds the whole line together. Fourth, the test. In Matthew, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Dignity gets tested at the edges, with the people easiest to overlook. The newborn and the dying. The man asleep in a doorway. The coworker nobody says good morning to.
screen: `MADE TO GOD'S IMAGE.` · `DIGNITY ISN'T EARNED OR LOST.` · `FROM CONCEPTION TO NATURAL DEATH.` · then, large: `ONE OF THESE MY LEAST BRETHREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to treat one person today with special dignity. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you'll cross today who is easy to overlook. The cashier. The person who cleans the office after everyone leaves. An elderly neighbor. Someone you're annoyed with. Hold their face for a moment. Then choose one concrete thing: their name used, eye contact held, a real question asked and the answer actually heard. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Life and dignity. The Church's first principle here: every person is made in God's image, and every life is to be protected from conception to natural death. Today's word.
Your line: every life. Today, when you catch yourself sorting someone as unimportant, stop and give them the crown back. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Catholics act on this teaching through pro-life ministries, hospice and hospital care, prison visiting, work against human trafficking, and campaigns against the death penalty; some parishes keep days of prayer for the dignity of life.

fork.setup: you're the psalm singer under the night sky, moon and stars overhead. you ask what a human being is. what's the psalm's answer?
options: a little less than the angels, crowned with glory.
fork.reveal: a little less than the angels, crowned with glory. the question starts small and the answer ends with a crown.

original.note: Latin: image of God. the Church's phrase for what Genesis says every person is made in.

trapdoor: what you thought: dignity means looking dignified.
what it means: a worth every person has from God, from conception to natural death, that nothing can earn or erase.
what a scholar hears: the Second Vatican Council listing attacks on it side by side, abortion and euthanasia next to slavery and disgraceful working conditions.

notes: Psalm 8 verse numbers in the Douay-Rheims: confirm 8:5 and 8:6 for the two quoted lines.
'The Catechism now calls the death penalty inadmissible' reflects the revised CCC 2267; 'now' is used without a date under the claims rule. Confirm wording.
Gaudium et Spes 27 paraphrased: list includes abortion, euthanasia, slavery, the selling of women and children, disgraceful working conditions. Confirm the selection is fair.
'Some Catholics give their energy to one end of that span and some to another' is descriptive and ranks no one; a Keeper may prefer different wording on a politically sensitive point.
CCC 356/GS 24: 'the only creature on earth that God has willed for its own sake' is paraphrased without the superlative.
